title: SICA: local editing and symbol navigation

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: LiveCodeBench participates in one mixed-task evolution run. The seed already has subagents and file-context management but modifies files only through whole-file overwrites.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Whole-file overwrites are extended with diff- and range-based editing, followed by a Python AST symbol locator in iteration 9. Appendix D's update sequence also reports a SmartEditor InputNormalizer (update 6), reduced diff-context output (8 and 13), MainAgent detection and routing of editing tasks (10), and AST parsing restricted to relevant code regions instead of entire files (14). These change the reusable editing interface and the amount of code processed or returned.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: These are reported implemented updates; retention in the final utility-winning agent remains unconfirmed. The normalizer's exact transformations were not independently checked in code. The 15-round run combines 50 SWE tasks, 50 LiveCodeBench tasks and synthetic editing/navigation tasks; synthetic navigation mainly motivates the AST tool. No individual ablation establishes the effect of these updates, and their appearance in two benchmark records is not independent replication. The seed's XML tool-call format, subagents and context management are inherited capabilities.

sources.locator: §3, §3.1; §4 Figure 3/Table 1; Appendix A–C; Appendix D, updates 6, 8–10, 13–14

title: TTHE: verification only after exposed failures

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Test-time adaptation uses a recent hard subset of 60 LiveCodeBench problems, starting from a ReAct scaffold without the reported conditional verification-and-repair route; the release window is unspecified.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The selected scaffold retains a low-cost solving path and adds verification and repair when public tests fail. Additional execution is thus conditional on an observed failure, rather than required for every problem.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The route is reported as retained. Adaptation and scoring use the same batch, making this a transductive result rather than a sealed generalization test. There is no individual-change ablation. The SWE empty-patch retry and DS-1000 tasks in the shared configuration do not establish additional LiveCodeBench mechanisms.

title: Darwin Gödel Machine: recoverable edits and candidate delivery

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Aider Polyglot evolution starts from bash, a whole-file editor and one agent attempt. Optimization uses 60 problems; 165 further problems support generalization evaluation.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The retained implementation adds replacement, insertion, range editing and undo, plus up to three attempts with workspace resets. Patch/test summaries inform later attempts; execution success and test counts guide selection, after which the selected patch is replayed. Local revision becomes recoverable, while candidate exploration is separated from final delivery.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The full-benchmark score increases from 14.2% to 30.7% (Section 4.4). This includes the optimization subset and measures the complete lineage, not either mechanism in isolation. Appendix F.2 gives the retained code, but its diff has not been linked to a repository commit. Internal tests do not access private ground truth. The coarse seed interface is a documented limitation, not an isolated failure-trace experiment.

sources.locator: Appendix F.2: SolutionAttempt/run_tests/forward; tools/edit.py; HTML L3622–4395

title: EvolveNet: separating library-specific and shared behavior

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: DS-1000 evolution starts from a 17-line shared seed program, before client-specific improvements are merged.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The round-2 example keeps schema preanalysis inside the Pandas branch while moving broadly applicable execution retries into shared cross-library logic. The merge preserves the intended scope of each client specialization.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: This is a reported merge discovery, not independently inspected final source; final retention remains unconfirmed. The protocol uses local feedback, server validation and held-out tests, but supplies no causal ablation of this merge. The Pandas-specific example does not establish a concrete discovery on SWE or LiveCodeBench, nor does a short seed alone identify a particular tool architecture.

title: AFlow: composing generation, selection and conditional repair

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: MBPP search begins with an empty workflow template and manually predefined operators. The LLM revises reusable code and prompts using parent workflows, modification history and execution feedback.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The selected round-14 program generates three candidates, selects with ScEnsemble and invokes Test. Failed tests route their output to FIX_CODE_PROMPT for repair. The evolved object is this executable composition and its conditional branch, rather than a newly invented operator or a single task answer.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Each candidate receives five validation runs, and the cited listing is the retained best MBPP program. The failure branch passes the problem, failed solution and returned test error to the repair prompt; the listing returns the repaired candidate without a further test call. A separate test-generation example is not this final chain. Component-level causal gains are not established, and the workflow must not be relabeled as HumanEval's selected implementation.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: The EvoAgentBench LiveCode setting starts from a vanilla harness that can return an empty turn after reasoning exceeds its budget. The precise initial implementation is unspecified.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: A retained recovery branch disables thinking only after runaway reasoning prevents output from resuming. Ordinary execution keeps its original reasoning mode, so the change is event-triggered recovery rather than globally disabling thinking or uniformly expanding the budget.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Training and test data are separate, with one sealed test after training-based selection. The relationship between EvoAgentBench LiveCode and official LiveCodeBench, including release alignment, remains unverified. The recovery example cannot be assigned to official LiveCodeBench or Terminal-Bench, and it does not isolate the causal contribution of the branch from the complete harness.

title: MermaidFlow: inheriting testing and candidate diversity

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: HumanEval search represents workflows as editable Mermaid graphs over supplied operators. The illustrated crossover starts from two existing parent workflows, not a newly identified universal seed.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Workflow_8 combines the test node introduced by Workflow_4 with Workflow_5's more diverse ensemble. Verification and candidate diversity can therefore be inherited from different parents through executable graph composition.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Section 5.4 and Figure 4 document this generated child. Appendix B.3 separately provides a selected HumanEval implementation; the crossover child is not automatically that final winner. The reported score does not isolate the testing node's effect, and the operators themselves are supplied rather than evolved by this example.

title: FlowEvo: reusing skills directly or as construction context

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: HumanEval and MBPP use generated workflows augmented by a persistent skill bank. Successful executions can supply procedures for subsequent tasks; Appendix A separates bank growth from frozen-bank MBPP evaluation.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Acquired skills can execute directly when compatible, or provide structured context for constructing a new workflow. This changes what is retained between problems and how the next solver uses it.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: On the 71 exact-transfer cases, direct reuse reaches 85.9% versus 81.7% for dynamic generation with lower token use; text memory reaches 87.3% at higher cost. No router pair separates significantly on the full evaluation split. These comparisons support conditional reuse, not universal replay superiority or a final coding-specific skill lineage. The detailed ALFWorld listing is not a coding artifact.

title: Darwin Gödel Machine: editing, patch selection and context recovery

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: SWE-bench evolution begins with a fixed model, bash and whole-file editing. Test execution and test summarization are already seed capabilities.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The best lineage adds line-range viewing and unique string replacement. Appendix F.1's added is_patch_valid rejects empty or whitespace-only patches, patches with no parsed modified files, and changes classified as test-only by a filename heuristic. The execution loop resets the workspace and supplies the failure reason before another attempt, with up to three attempts in total. It also compares candidates with internal tests and summarizes older messages after context overflow before resuming. Testing itself is inherited; the evolved changes govern its use and the recovery paths.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The changes are reported as retained. Screening on 10+50 tasks precedes evaluation on 200 tasks that include those screening tasks; this is not an independent 500-task test. No individual causal ablations apportion the overall gain among the changes. Context summarization does not guarantee preservation of every earlier tool result.

title: SICA: extending the inherited editing interface

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: SWE-bench Verified shares one mixed-task run with LiveCodeBench and synthetic tasks. The seed already contains subagents, an asynchronous overseer and file-context management, but editing is limited to overwriting files.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Evolution adds diff- and range-based editing, followed by an AST symbol locator in iteration 9. Appendix D further records editor-input normalization, task-based edit routing, smaller diff-context returns and parsing only relevant AST regions; the program-generation entry gives the update numbers. The existing subagents, overseer and XML tool-call parser are inherited architecture.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The fixed 50-task SWE subset participates in a 15-iteration mixed-task run, not an independent repository-only search. These are reported implemented discoveries whose retention in the final utility winner has not been verified from its diff. Overall SWE improvements cannot be assigned to individual changes, and the AST discovery is primarily associated with synthetic navigation tasks.

title: Multi-task Self-Harness: one lineage across three repository settings

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: The seed is a 49-line prompt-and-bash loop that appends raw outputs without timeouts, compression or recovery. SWE-Bench Pro contributes 60 evolution tasks and 100 held-out tasks from a pool of 731. Verified (100 tasks) and DeepSWE (53 tasks) are frozen out-of-distribution evaluations, excluded from evolution.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Outputs previously appended verbatim are bounded: above 48,000 characters, the harness preserves the beginning and end and inserts a notice suggesting a narrower command or saving output to a file. Outputs older than the latest six are shortened to at most 6,000 characters. These rules appear in iteration 1 and remain in the selected iteration 5. Separate history compaction preserves opening and recent messages, and a fresh-context completion review checks the task against the filesystem.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Section 5.2 reports that the seed aborts on 12 SWE-Bench Pro tasks because test or build output exceeds the input limit; iteration 5 solves seven of them. This is a complete-version comparison, not an ablation of truncation. The same lineage serves all three settings, so they are not independent discoveries. History compaction rarely triggers in coding; it is distinct from per-output trimming. The iteration-6 budget cap is excluded. DeepSWE currently has no second extracted study supplying a concrete change for comparison.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Three independent model-specific searches on a 100-task SWE-bench Verified subset start from a minimal DeepAgent harness. Seed MiniMax and Qwen traces make changes but stop without completing executable verification.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: MiniMax separates empty-diff inspection from targeted testing through two subagents. Qwen combines a patch verifier with pre-submission diff/test instructions. In GLM, build_verification_instruction previously requested test execution and debugging on failure. The evolved instructions distinguish missing imports or dependencies, ask the agent to install the missing package and rerun the exact test, and resume source debugging only if it still fails. This is a retained instruction change, not a programmatic gate enforcing that sequence.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The modifications are retained in separate promoted harnesses. Appendix B.2 reports successful verification in the paired MiniMax and Qwen traces. Its GLM Astropy case (Figure 16) moves from syntax-only checking to dependency repair and executable verification: all four previously failing FAIL-TO-PASS tests then pass. These are whole-harness case comparisons, not ablations of particular instructions or subagents. Table 1 separately gives MiniMax overall Pass of 46.0% versus 52.5%. Both 67 held-in and 33 held-out tasks may affect acceptance, so the latter are not an untouched test set. These are separate searches within one paper, not frozen transfers from Terminal-Bench.

title: TTHE: treating an empty patch as a rerun condition

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Test-time adaptation on a 40-task hard SWE-bench Verified slice begins with stock mini-swe-agent, whose first attempt can terminate with an empty patch.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The adapted scaffold reruns an empty-patch attempt with explicit reproduce–localize–repair–retest instructions and increases the step budget during multiround search. The change converts an otherwise terminal outcome into a conditional recovery path.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The selected mechanism is reported as retained. Selection without gold labels and subsequent scoring use the same batch, so this is transductive adaptation rather than unseen-task generalization. The budget and instructions change together. LiveCodeBench's public-test mechanism is not assigned to SWE, and the example's small-patch constraint is not general repository-repair advice.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Search on SWE-bench Verified starts from a short prompt and shell tool, without memory, middleware, skills or subagents. The split contains 50 search and 450 evaluation tasks, with additional cross-model evaluation.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Retained memory adds conditional guidance for identifying responsibility along execution paths and covering affected callers when changing shared interfaces. An ungated control instead accumulates more task-specific repair records.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The examples are reusable guidance, not enforced tool behavior. They support a distinction between conditional repair knowledge and memorized fixes, but neither rule has an independent ablation. Gains from the complete structure and guidance tracks cannot be attributed to memory alone. Evaluation on unseen tasks does not make the two rules independent discoveries.

title: AHE: transferring execution and delivery controls

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: All 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks evaluate frozen transfer from Terminal-Bench 2 evolution. The source seed, NexAU_0, exposes only bash and has no middleware, skills or long-term memory.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The transferred harness exposes per-call timeouts, protects accepted artifacts from destructive actions, forwards cross-step risk reminders to the next model turn, and checks acceptance criteria before completion. These occupy distinct tool, interception, context and completion modules; reminders are not equivalent to execution-level blocking.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The changes are reported as retained, but every concrete edit was discovered in the terminal source domain. They are not SWE discoveries. One lineage introduces interacting components, and no isolated SWE contribution is established for any single mechanism. Frozen transfer therefore supports reuse of the complete harness, not independent evolution on another benchmark.

title: DarwinX: transferring artifact and acceptance guidance

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: SWE-bench Verified is a 500-task frozen transfer target after skill evolution on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The source seed is base Monet without the seven later verification/artifact skills.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The retained bundle extracts acceptance contracts, grounds deliverables in real tool results, checks and repairs artifacts, repeats checks after modifications, and repairs safety/interface-contract violations before completion.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The seven skills are jointly selected execution guidance, not separately ablated mechanisms or an unavoidable submission blocker. The bundle's SWE evaluation does not show where the skills were discovered. Terminal-Bench, TerminalWorld and different model configurations have distinct protocols; evidence from those configurations must not be merged into a single repository evolution run.

title: Mixture of Self-Improving Branches: retrieval before the first action

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: SWE-bench Lite uses mini-swe-agent as its original baseline. The immediate parent of the illustrated modification already has structured editing; the 300 tasks are split into 50 development and 250 test tasks.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The candidate extracts up to eight issue identifiers, ranks files by matches, reads two source files and one test file, and injects bounded content into the initial message. This changes initialization through targeted retrieval, rather than adding the parent's existing unique-match replacement tool.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Appendix E.4 supplies a discovery example; retention in the final deployed head is unverified. Development-selected heads and test-best candidates are reported separately and must not be conflated. The example does not establish an individual causal gain or a universal best retrieval budget.

title: RHO: connecting requirements to executable verification

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: SWE-Bench Pro uses a domain-specific optimization from vanilla Codex, before its repair-verify helper and requirements ledger. It is not a frozen transfer of the terminal configuration.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: A retained callable helper finds toolchains outside PATH, runs lightweight language checks, reports generated artifacts and accepts custom verification commands. A separate requirements ledger is revisited before submission.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The setup draws 100 training and 100 held-out tasks from the ScaleAI test set using evaluator revision 0c64e26f00b9. Held-out trajectories show helper calls, distinguishing this configuration from the unexecuted terminal scripts. No single-change ablation isolates the helper, and terminal playbook findings cannot be substituted for these repository observations.

title: OneRecipe: timed reminders for language-specific verification

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Multi-SWE-Bench evolution runs by language and model from a minimal mini-SWE plugin: a short prompt, bash, and empty hooks and memory. Full mini-SWE is a separate baseline; evaluation also considers cross-language transfer.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The retained C++/Haiku example uses before_query to detect recent testing or submission cues and inject compilation/testing reminders. Prompts and memory constrain patch scope, discourage test-file edits and request targeted verification.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The procedure uses three rounds, 80 steps and USD 1.5 per rollout. The hook nudges rather than blocks submission. make/ctest depend on the language ecosystem, and the test-file restriction reflects the hidden gold-test-patch convention. Aggregate transfer results do not isolate the contribution of either guidance content or trigger timing.

title: CODESKILL: task procedures and event-triggered diagnostics

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: A separately trained manager maintains natural-language skills around frozen coding policies. EnvBench uses a ReAct-style agent and SWE-bench Verified uses mini-SWE-agent; both expose bash-based actions.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The published merged Maven task-level skill distinguishes environment, configuration and dependency failures before code edits. Its merged event-level counterpart diagnoses a missing test-jar, checks its producing module, arranges generation/installation, and verifies the artifact before retrying the build. Persistent updates change skill instructions, not the supplied tools.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: These are bank examples rather than individually scored skill ablations. Project build-file edits are downstream actions, not evolved harness code. The test tasks are held out from manager-policy training, but Section 4.1 constructs their skill bank in two preparatory passes: extraction from no-skill runs, then evolution from skill-conditioned runs. Final evaluation filters out skills whose recorded provenance includes the current instance. This is test-set bank preparation, not evaluation of an unchanged training-only bank; benchmark gains do not isolate either Maven example.

title: GSE: generalizing diagnostic skills across repositories

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent are evaluated on bug-revealing test generation for 108 Java bugs derived from Multi-SWE-Bench, and false-positive filtering for 500 IndustrialBugs reports. These settings evaluate defect analysis, not patch resolution.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Figure 3 consolidates narrow collection-size and permission rules into a skill distinguishing value-triggered from state-triggered defects, linked to existing test-construction skills. The filtering case replaces conflicting project-specific nullability rules with reasoning about nullability guarantees and propagates that abstraction to related skills.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: One-project-held-out evaluation tests reuse across repositories. The examples illustrate learned abstraction and compatibility between skills. Aggregate results and architecture-level ablations do not isolate either example's causal effect, and the simplified Figure 3 illustration should not be treated as a full final-bank artifact.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Before real issues are presented, synthetic issue solving acquires project-specific skills associated with repository entities. The downstream repair agent retrieves this knowledge rather than rewriting its controller during the illustrated repair.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: In Django-11206, the acquired guidance steers the agent away from an exponent heuristic toward the existing Decimal pipeline, precision-dependent numerical equivalence and boundary-case checks.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The paired traces in Section IV-E pass 0/2 and 2/2 fail-to-pass tests without and with skills. This demonstrates an application of acquired knowledge, not a separate causal estimate for each instruction. The persistent object is entity-grounded guidance; the particular code patch is a task output. Knowledge acquisition and downstream repair therefore remain distinct stages.

title: Meta-Harness: discovering the environment before reasoning

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Terminal-Bench 2.0 search and evaluation share 89 tasks. Search considers Terminus 2 and Terminus-KIRA; the illustrated discovery builds on KIRA, inheriting native tool calling, a 30KB output cap and a completion checklist.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The retained bootstrap gathers directory contents, language/package-manager versions and memory before the first model call, then injects a snapshot into the initial context. A 15-second timeout and silent failure keep the startup probe from blocking execution.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Appendix B.3 reports gains on seven tasks relative to KIRA, especially where specialized tools are needed, and identifies two to four initial environment-discovery turns as the bottleneck. This within-benchmark comparison supplies no independent coding holdout and is not an isolated causal ablation. The inherited checklist and output cap are not new discoveries; the public author artifact identifies version 2.0.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Terminal-Bench 2.0 evolution uses 89 tasks for ten iterations. NexAU_0 begins with bash, a default five-minute shell timeout, and no middleware, skills or long-term memory; SWE is reserved for frozen transfer.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Retained edits expose command-specific timeouts, protect validated artifacts, detect cross-step risks, inject next-turn reminders and check completion. In configure-git-webserver, an intermediate overrideable guard still permits cleanup to erase a working deployment. Paired iteration-8 updates harden the guard and make warnings salient before the next action.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: That task changes from 0/2 to 2/2 successful rollouts, with destructive cleanup blocked and the live state submitted. This supports the reported mechanism without separating the paired edits. Manifests and commits identify changes, but the historical run has not been reproduced. Components interact non-additively, and Section 4.4.1 reports costs from redundant checks on long-horizon tasks. The current official configuration corroborates version 2.0.

title: ModularRSI: correcting tool dispatch and completion state

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: An initial modular harness evolves on related tasks outside Terminal-Bench, then undergoes frozen evaluation on version 2.0. The separate Section 6.4 method comparison specifies Terminus-2 and does not establish that seed for every main experiment.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: In Appendix D.4's Go repair case, the initial dispatcher rejects multiline write_file input and sends it to the shell, producing a command-not-found error. The reported revision identifies write_file or edit_block by command name and sends the remaining payload to the editing helper. The paper reports promotion in generation 9 and unchanged multiline handling in generation 12. A separate loop update re-presents pending acceptance conditions when the agent signals completion without commands.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: On the same Go task, three runs per version all succeed; their interaction counts (called episodes in the source) change from [41,24,43] to [26,18,31], reducing the mean from 36 to 25. These are external evolution-task observations, not Terminal-Bench test cases or an isolated dispatcher ablation: parser recovery and other changes occur concurrently. A source check of the released merged module finds the editing-command branch nested under a cat-only condition, making that branch unreachable for the editing names in this snapshot. This is not the historical generation 9/12 artifact; those source snapshots and original rollouts remain unchecked. The current code therefore does not independently confirm the paper-reported fix or invalidate its historical observations.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Separate model searches use 64 filtered Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks. The minimal DeepAgent seed provides read, write, edit and shell tools plus the default task prompt, without the later runtime limits.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: MiniMax's final harness encourages early creation of required artifacts and redirects stalled work through a total tool-message cap. Qwen instead adds dependency/artifact checks, retry discipline, loop recovery and middleware triggered by tool errors.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: These are retained changes in different promoted harnesses, not one shared patch. Held-out trajectories are withheld from diagnosis, but held-out scores participate in the promotion regression gate, so evaluation is not sealed. This entry records only the extracted MiniMax and Qwen terminal changes; GLM's repository dependency-recovery mechanism must not be transferred to this setting.

title: Mixture of Self-Improving Branches: checking completion once

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Terminal-Bench 2.0 uses 88 tasks split into 30 development and 58 test tasks. The illustrated candidate's immediate parent is verification-enhanced Terminus-KIRA with an existing tool-execution loop.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The first completion signal triggers a verification prompt and sets a one-time flag. Subsequent tool use leaves the flag intact, so a later completion exits without reopening the same verification request.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Appendix E.3 documents a discovered candidate, not a confirmed final head deployed by the router. Its retained state flag bounds repeated checking, but final retention and an isolated effect are unverified. Test-best candidates in the discovery pool must remain distinct from development-selected results. The parent's verification capabilities are inherited rather than new mechanisms.

title: Multi-task Self-Harness: bounded observations and fresh-context review

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Mixed-task evolution includes 60 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, with 29 held out. The seed is a 49-line prompt-and-bash Python loop that accumulates outputs verbatim without compaction or recovery.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Iteration 5 retains the beginning and end of long outputs, further shortens old observations, and trims overlong history to its opening and recent messages. Instructions allow recovery of omitted information from files. The first stop decision opens a fresh-context review of the original task and current filesystem.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: These changes are reported as retained and reused across tasks, not rediscovered independently for each benchmark. History trimming rarely triggers in coding, and candidates are not screened by validation score. The 150-second/eight-call cap added at iteration 6 is excluded from this iteration-5 account; no individual-change ablation is established.

title: RRSI: bounding audits and waiting behavior

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Evolution uses all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, beginning with Terminus-2 before the reported bounded audit and polling guidance. This record concerns candidate R0-A only.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: R0-A adds a bounded completion audit and nonblocking polling guidance for long-running work. Both are jointly accepted at that iteration, modifying how the agent checks completion and waits for results.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Acceptance at R0 is documented, but survival in the final harness is unknown. The polling mechanism is guidance, not evidence of a scheduler rewrite. Rejected candidates are not included among the evolved features. SWE does not participate in selection, and this within-benchmark acceptance does not establish held-out generalization or separate effects for the two instructions.

title: DarwinX: making delivery requirements explicit in skills

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Evolution and evaluation use the same 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks. Base Monet starts without the seven later verification/artifact-contract skills.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The retained bundle extracts acceptance conditions, checks artifact paths, formats and values, repairs failures and rechecks after changes. It also requires real tool evidence and addresses safety/interface constraints before completion.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The authors describe seven jointly selected skills, not per-skill causal ablations. Their content guides execution rather than demonstrating unavoidable submission gates. TerminalWorld uses a separate train/test protocol, and SWE is a transfer target; neither supplies additional evolution evidence for this terminal entry. Whole-bundle results therefore cannot be assigned independently to each instruction.

title: RHO: organizing terminal work through a requirements playbook

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: A terminal-specific optimization uses 30 training and 59 held-out tasks, starting from vanilla Codex with GPT-5.5 high in a configurable workspace. The paper names Terminal-Bench 2 and pins commit 53ff2b87d621 without an established minor-version mapping.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: A retained playbook records task requirements, organizes host-to-container commands, checks final artifacts at their container paths and revisits the specification before completion. Scripts are generated alongside it.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Behavioral analysis explicitly reports that terminal trajectories do not run those scripts; the operative observed change is guidance. SWE-Bench Pro's executed repair-verify helper must not be assigned here. Cross-benchmark reuse and an individual causal effect are unproven. This setting remains version 2.x, minor version unspecified, rather than being silently assigned to 2.0 or 2.1.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Terminal-Bench 2 is held out from skill-manager policy training and evaluated through mini-SWE-agent with frozen downstream model weights. The paper does not establish a minor version for this record.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The learned manager extracts task-level and event-driven instructions and maintains the bank through additions, revisions, merges and removals. Section 4.1 specifies two preparatory passes over the test set before final evaluation: initial extraction, followed by skill-conditioned evolution. During final evaluation, skills whose tracked provenance includes the current task are excluded. Transfer therefore concerns the manager with test-set bank preparation; it is neither a training-only frozen bank nor a demonstrated streaming update after each final-evaluation query.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: This supports terminal evaluation coverage and an update mechanism. The published Maven examples demonstrate skill granularity but are not tied to particular terminal tasks or a terminal-specific final harness. Accordingly, no terminal-specific content or individual mechanism gain is inferred from them; policy training, bank evolution and task execution remain separate processes.

title: AIDE²: search diversity and bounded experiment history

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: MLE-bench Lite22 is a held-out transfer evaluation of AIDE85, evolved on external tasks. Its AIDE0 ancestor greedily selects the best candidate and accumulates full candidate histories during drafting and improvement.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The retained runtime searches multiple strategy arms with periodic cross-arm forks. It summarizes initial and recent solutions, adds selected error signatures when bugs recur, catches nearly empty code and prompts generalization to unseen test data. Search can change strategy while retaining a strong candidate.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Mean private percentile rises from 0.678 ± 0.006 to 0.722 ± 0.011; errors are one standard error. End-of-run median prompt-size reduction reaches 7×. These are whole-runtime transfer results, not module ablations, and AIDE47 scores higher on this benchmark (0.730 ± 0.005). Lite22 never enters evolutionary selection. The ineffective ranking penalty, rejected ensembles and scoring-script repair are not retained task-runtime mechanisms in this account.

signals.scope: AIDE85 versus AIDE0 on MLE-bench Lite22; not a claim that AIDE85 beats every intermediate checkpoint.
signals.summary: The complete retained runtime improves over the ancestor; individual edits are not causally isolated, and AIDE47 scores higher on this benchmark.
signals.evidence_quote: These are whole-runtime transfer results, not module ablations, and AIDE47 scores higher on this benchmark (0.730 ± 0.005).

title: SIA: turning denoising experiments into structured feedback

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: The MAGIC denoising hyperparameter task starts from a Meta-Agent-generated system prompt, single-tool dispatch loop and output parser around gpt-oss-120b. It is task-specific harness iteration, not MLE-bench evaluation.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: With model weights fixed, the Feedback-Agent adds a batched configuration driver and a parser exposing parameter–score pairs. These reusable tools organize experiments and their feedback; particular neighbor counts, diffusion steps, bandwidths and preprocessing choices are task-level candidates rather than harness changes.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Section 7.2 reports the discoveries but provides no final-version diff or individual-tool ablation, leaving final retention unconfirmed. Table 2 specifies no separate train/test split for this task. Later GRPO updates and postprocessing belong to the weight-update phase and are excluded from this harness-only record.

title: AIBuildAI-2: carrying experiment takeaways into future runs

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: MLE-bench and live competitions use a hierarchical ML agent initialized with a human-authored topical index and roughly 1,000 knowledge documents in about 30 categories.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: After a task, an L2 builder turns the working directory into a categorized takeaway document. An L1 builder revises the category's instruction and its pointers to L2 documents; the top-level category index remains fixed. A second stream incorporates external material, and future executions retrieve relevant guidance selectively.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The paper specifies this persistent-update procedure but does not expose a complete before/after post-run document with an isolated evaluation. System-level results do not establish the effect of a particular evolved instruction. The trained models or ensembles produced during competitions are task outputs, distinct from changes to the agent's reusable knowledge.

sources.locator: Figure 1; Methods: Knowledge builder agents and Knowledge system evolution

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: MLE-bench uses a fixed Codex runtime and repository-grounded guidance constructed for each competition. The initial plan scopes needed capabilities and collects relevant sources while excluding the original competition webpage and competition-specific content.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Diagnostic trials produce logs and results that drive repeated revisions of modeling, preprocessing, training and checking guidance. Final skills are descriptive and exclude runnable training/inference scripts; the resulting graph is frozen for downstream execution.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Appendix A.2.1 separates construction/exploration from the matched running budget. Construction already encounters the task, so this is not unseen-task transfer. The retained object is operational knowledge around a fixed controller, not an evolved Codex runtime or a particular trained model. Reported results do not isolate the contribution of an individual ML rule.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Search on MGSM starts from an archive containing supplied agent designs, rather than a single named seed.

sections.label: Discovered behavior
sections.text: The example named Verified Multimodal Agent generates a representation of the problem, passes it to a second module for feedback and revision, and conditions the final reasoning module on that revised representation. The listing passes textual fields; the name alone does not establish an image-processing pipeline.

sections.label: Outcome and scope
sections.text: This is a documented discovered agent, not the paper's highest-scoring named agent. Table 2 separately evaluates the top three MGSM agents on GSM8K and GSM-Hard; Appendix A adds SVAMP and ASDiv. Those transfer scores cannot be assigned to Code 6's mechanism.

title: AFlow: selecting and checking candidate answers

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: GSM8K search starts from an empty workflow template with supplied generation, selection and programming operators; their later call order is not part of the seed.

sections.label: Discovered behavior
sections.text: The selected program generates five solutions, selects with ScEnsemble, and invokes Programmer for a computational review, falling back to the selected solution if no output is produced.

sections.label: Outcome and scope
sections.text: Figure 6 traces accepted additions and prompt refinements. The operators are supplied; their composition is searched. The reported workflow is retained, but its aggregate score does not isolate each addition.

title: MermaidFlow: computational candidates and final formatting

sections.label: Setting and artifact
sections.text: The published GSM8K workflow combines one textual solution with five Programmer outputs produced under different analysis instructions, selects with ScEnsemble, then invokes Programmer to refine and format the selected answer.

sections.label: Comparison and limits
sections.text: Relative to AFlow's post-selection computational review, this artifact places computational generation before selection as well. The listing supports this composition, not a claim that all calls execute in parallel or that each added call improves accuracy independently.

title: FlowEvo: carrying useful procedures across problems

sections.label: Settings and update
sections.text: GSM8K and MATH-500 evaluate a workflow generator augmented with a persistent skill bank. Successful procedures are compiled and can be retrieved as context for later workflow generation.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The paper identifies skill-conditioned generation as the relevant reuse mode for code and math. It does not provide the same detailed mathematical skill lineage as its ALFWorld example. We therefore record a supported accumulation mechanism and mathematical evaluation, rather than inventing a particular evolved mathematical tactic or attributing ALFWorld's replay gains to mathematics.

title: AFlow: combining programmatic and textual solutions

sections.label: Documented artifact
sections.text: From the same template family, a separate MATH workflow executes a program, rewrites its output as a solution, generates three textual alternatives, and selects among the four with ScEnsemble. This is the published selected workflow for the level-5 setting, not a frozen transfer of its GSM8K procedure.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Search uses 250 OlympiadBench / hard Omni-MATH problems and zero-shot, few-shot, and ACE initializations.

sections.label: Discovered behavior
sections.text: The selected BM25 harness routes by mathematical subject. Combinatorics deduplicates and reranks examples; geometry combines a hard reference with lexical neighbors; number theory favors explicit techniques; the default route adjusts example count. Two search lineages contribute to the merged policy.

sections.label: Outcome and scope
sections.text: A frozen harness is evaluated on 200 unseen IMO-AnswerBench, IMO-ProofBench, and ArXivMath problems: average accuracy is 38.8%, versus 34.1% without retrieval. Evaluation includes the search backbone and four unseen models. These are whole-policy results, not independent ablations of routing rules or formally checked proofs.

title: Co-Harness: repairing execution before adding diversity

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: The reported AIME24 case starts from a failing code-interpreter configuration.

sections.label: Discovered behavior
sections.text: Changes repair launch settings and process cleanup, batch inference, restore thinking on follow-up turns, and combine trajectories from two seeds by majority vote. Later prompt changes regress and are rolled back.

sections.label: Outcome and scope
sections.text: The final ensemble is reported within the time budget. We do not reproduce the claimed speedup: the stated ratio disagrees with the accompanying times. Appendix H also describes 90 questions despite the AIME24 label. These ambiguities limit quantitative interpretation, while the sequence of runtime edits is explicit. The separate AIME24/25 and HMMT25 co-evolution results also include model training.

title: HarnessBank: matching recovery to the backbone

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: EvoAgentBench's Omni-MATH setting uses a study-specific vanilla harness and disjoint training/test tasks.

sections.label: Discovered behavior
sections.text: For the Qwen backbone, recovery disables thinking after a runaway rather than on every call. The evolved stack transfers to another Qwen model, but does not help Gemini's different failure pattern; its matched intervention increases reasoning instead.

sections.label: Outcome and scope
sections.text: Table 1 reports test success rising from 54.3% to 66.0% for the selected Qwen harness. Cross-model results support a failure-dependent intervention, not a universal setting. The full stack's gain is not attributed to the recovery switch alone.

title: MermaidFlow: diversified solvers followed by refinement

sections.label: Setting and artifact
sections.text: The published MATH workflow obtains five Custom responses under distinct solver/outline instructions and one Programmer result, selects with ScEnsemble, and sends the selection to a refinement call. Its reusable object is the operator graph and associated prompts.

sections.label: Comparison and limits
sections.text: Like AFlow, it combines textual and programmatic candidates, but the supplied composition and final refinement differ. The shared use of AFlow-derived operators makes this a related design lineage, not a fully independent invention of those operators.

title: Mixture of Self-Improving Branches: constructive checks and disagreement resolution

sections.label: Setting and search
sections.text: Olympiad-level math uses Meta-Harness-based branch search with changing development subsets and proposal guidance. The reported Math–Gemini branches differentiate concrete answer checking and proof-obligation routing from solution construction and agreement challenges.

sections.label: Concrete candidate
sections.text: Appendix E.1's gap_directed_construction retrieves worked examples using a plan, rehearses a reference to produce a calibration note, and separates constructing an attainable answer from deriving necessary conditions. Agreement triggers a challenge; disagreement triggers a concrete check before adjudication.

sections.label: Selection limit
sections.text: Appendix E describes retrospectively test-best candidates from a development-ranked pool. Its 58% candidate score is not the score of the development-selected deployed head. The mechanism is documented, but those selection protocols are not interchangeable.

title: WDA: distributing refinement across selected stages

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: LiveBench Math extends this category to challenging informal mathematical reasoning, rather than a named olympiad. Search starts from a minimal solver prompt and can revise instructions or split them across stages.

sections.label: Selected structure
sections.text: The published Qwen search selects two stages, [P11, P12], while the GPT search selects three, [P2, P3, P10], with their ancestries reported separately. These are fixed-per-task pipelines, not a runtime policy choosing depth for each question.

sections.label: Outcome and limits
sections.text: The reported selected test scores are 68.85% and 63.93%, respectively. They support selected pipeline structures, not a universal benefit from longer refinement or an isolated effect of any one stage.

title: WHALE: making tool use effective through joint updates

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: A study-specific tool-integrated math harness and Qwen3.5-2B are optimized using DAPO-Math-17K subsets and tested on AIME 2024/2025.

sections.label: Observed contrast
sections.text: The Appendix D.2 base trace never uses the interpreter and exhausts its answer budget, whereas the final model–harness pair solves the same counting problem. Harness-only search has little effect from the initial pair; alternating weight updates and harness search improves the reported results.

sections.label: Attribution limit
sections.text: This is evidence about a co-evolved pair and its behavior, not a final harness-only diff proving which change caused tool use. It complements fixed-backbone harness studies but cannot be pooled with them as an independent pure-harness gain.

title: Self-modifying Lean agents: bounded repair and checked names

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: A single-attempt/check seed evolves on warm-up lemmas, miniF2F-valid and PutnamBench tasks.

sections.label: Discovered behavior
sections.text: The accepted lineage adds bounded compiler-guided repair, batched lemma-name checks, and verified signatures. On unknown-name or type errors, the workflow can exclude a bad name, return a checked alternative and retry. The c141 branch plans and proves auxiliary lemmas before attempting assembly, but mismatched lemma contexts, assembly failures and longer-prompt risks prevent this richer structure from becoming the strongest route. The winning c144 remains mainly a whole-proof repair workflow; its proof-context labels do not establish a fully verified dependency graph.

sections.label: Outcome and scope
sections.text: On 244 held-out miniF2F-test problems, c144 reaches 45.1%, versus 12.7% for the seed. This comparison includes curriculum coevolution and multiple edits; it does not isolate the lemma tools or demonstrate unrestricted proof-graph improvement.

title: RSI-Exam: proof extraction and use of limited checks

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: The fixed-model seed proposes a proof, checks it, and repairs once; each theorem permits three model calls and four Lean checks.

sections.label: Observed revisions
sections.text: GPT-5.6-sol and GLM 5.3 optimizer runs fix extraction that truncated nested proofs; other revisions add compiler repairs or alter diagnostics. These are optimizer identities, not the pinned task model. In the GLM run, visible accuracy rises from 8/54 to 13/54 after extraction repair and to 20/54 after a combined diagnostic/prompt change; later variants regress.

sections.label: Scope
sections.text: These are version-level observations from one official resource, not independent papers. Visible checkpoint scores are not hidden-test gains. Final retention of each component is not established by the summary alone.

title: Evolved prover interfaces: from compilation to interactive control

sections.label: Seed and retained changes
sections.text: Evolution starts from a Rocq MCP server exposing whole-file compilation. Retained additions include a persistent session with step/rollback/state interaction, a try tool that tests up to eight candidates and commits the first success, and error hints. A heavily used lemma-search proposal yields no accuracy gain and is rejected; exemplar retrieval is also rejected. File-manipulation and project-verification tools added for Phase 2 are supplied setup changes, not empirically selected mutations.

sections.label: Outcome and limits
sections.text: Held-out miniF2F-Rocq evaluation compares the resulting interface across four models. Its Lean port lowers cost/time per solve on a PutnamBench subset, but solves fewer problems than lean-lsp-mcp. Human setup and review remain; this is bounded interface evolution, not autonomous improvement of every system component.

signals.scope: Lemma-search proposal in interface evolution; no benchmark-specific effect size assigned.
signals.summary: Frequent use does not establish benefit: the lemma-search proposal is rejected without an accuracy gain.
signals.evidence_quote: A heavily used lemma-search proposal yields no accuracy gain and is rejected; exemplar retrieval is also rejected.

signals.scope: Lean port on the reported PutnamBench subset, compared with lean-lsp-mcp.
signals.summary: Lower cost/time per solve coexists with fewer solved problems; this is not uniformly better performance.
signals.evidence_quote: Its Lean port lowers cost/time per solve on a PutnamBench subset, but solves fewer problems than lean-lsp-mcp.

title: ProofEvolve: verified resources that persist across problems

sections.label: Seed and change
sections.text: The persistent schema library grows through extraction of kernel-checked subproofs; typed recombination exposes remaining premises as subgoals. This component-level accumulation is distinct from evolving a single target proof.

sections.label: Reuse evidence
sections.text: A controlled compositional study compares growing and reset libraries. A separate LeanWorkbook experiment retrieves self-generated verified proofs from disjoint source theorems, improving target success over no retrieval; random retrieval provides little benefit. That experiment supplies context for one whole-proof attempt, rather than testing typed DAG recombination. Its gain must not be attributed to every component of the full prover.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: LawBench charge prediction. Zero-shot, few-shot, ACE and MCE initializations.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The published classification frontier includes a two-call draft verifier: after an initial prediction from five similar examples, it retrieves five same-label confirmers and five different-label challengers, then asks whether to revise the draft. With fewer than five stored examples it falls back to a single few-shot call. The selected label-primed program instead combines one query-relevant example per label with nearby contrasting pairs in one prompt. These are alternative frontier programs, not successive stages of one final classifier.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: These are shared classification programs evaluated across datasets, not a separately discovered legal decision procedure. Search-set selection precedes held-out evaluation.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: LawBench. A fixed classifier receives a task prompt and the output of a query-to-context function; Algorithm 1 initializes learned context as empty. The initial pattern-extraction skill belongs to the context-engineering agent, not the classifier's execution harness.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The learned target-side context directs full-case reading, extraction of discrete acts, act-to-charge matching and validation. Its retrieval program always supplies format rules and the decomposition framework, adding warnings when structural markers suggest multiple acts. The separate skill that teaches the context engineer how to construct this artifact is an optimizer-side change.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The task-agent evidence is the reusable context and query-dependent retrieval program in Appendix D.4.3. The optimizer skill in D.4.2 is a distinct object. Neither individual guidance lines nor retrieval triggers are independently ablated; the LawBench configuration differs from other studies.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: LawBench, within the three-dataset classification search. Zero-shot and all-example few-shot harnesses in the Meta-Harness implementation.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The selected 20-percent-budget harness fuses word-bigram and character n-gram TF-IDF rankings, then downweights labels already represented while filling a bounded context.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: One shared classifier serves Law, S2D and USPTO. The proposed benefit of word phrases for legal cases is an explanatory hypothesis, not a separately ablated legal mechanism.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Law. No-memory and all-example few-shot configurations around GPT-OSS-120B.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The proposer recalibrates historical evidence against current component state and converts it into targeted edit intent; the study evaluates the selected evolved classifier on held-out legal examples.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The reviewed primary text does not expose a legal-specific final program diff. We count the reported evolution experiment, not a new legal reasoning rule or the optimizer design as a learned task mechanism.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Symptom2Disease (22 labels). The same classification seed family, evaluated on symptom descriptions.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Label-conditioned retrieval and query-local contrasting examples provide reusable alternatives to placing the complete accumulated history in context.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The same frontier programs described above are reused across classification datasets; this is not a second independent discovery. Held-out classification accuracy does not establish clinical validity.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Symptom2Disease. The same fixed-model query-to-context interface starts without learned context in Algorithm 1. The initial symptom-profile skill guides the context engineer; it is not itself the target classifier's prompt or tool.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The evolved target-side context contains distinctions between commonly confused labels. Its query-to-context program detects symptom patterns and returns relevant discriminator sections, falling back to the full guide if no condition matches. Separately, the optimizer's context-construction skill shifts from generalized profiles toward conservative evidence-backed additions and stopping criteria; those skill instructions are not executed by the target classifier.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Appendix D.3.3 exposes reusable classifier context and retrieval examples, but does not isolate their individual effects. The evidence and stopping thresholds in D.3.2 belong to the context optimizer's skill. They are neither target-runtime guards nor general diagnostic guidance.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Symptom2Disease. Zero-shot and all-example few-shot seeds.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Its selected shared classifier combines word and character retrieval and penalizes repeated-label coverage in the prompt.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: S2D has a separate held-out test set, but the artifact is shared with the legal and reaction-classification settings. The tokenizer explanation is not a clinical causal result.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: Symptom2Disease. No-memory and all-example few-shot configurations around GPT-OSS-120B.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Validation-guided evolution with recalibrated historical evidence produces a selected classifier evaluated on a separate S2D test split.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The experiment establishes task coverage; the reviewed text does not specify the final S2D retrieval implementation. Component-drift robustness is evidence about the optimizer, not a retained classifier feature.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Reported tool revisions add symptom-overlap or stronger lexical retrieval; across phases, tools and memory incorporate symptom extraction and label-grouped diagnostic indicators.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Training-time repair examples permit a second attempt, whereas phase-boundary review and final evaluation freeze committed files. Joint weight updates preclude interpreting the full gain as harness-only improvement.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: LoCoMo; MemBench. A BM25-only configuration around a fixed answering model, with semantic/structured views, name-stripped alternatives and query decomposition disabled.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Failure-log diagnosis activates name-stripped alternative retrieval and multi-hop query decomposition, then introduces a verification pass for low-confidence answers. The first two are described as dormant configuration capabilities rather than newly authored tools. Guarded updates can revert regressions; the evolved object is the retrieval/answer configuration.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Section 4.5 removes components and reruns evolution, providing procedure-level ablation evidence rather than a fixed-checkpoint edit test. Per-question failure logs provide supervision, so this is not label-free adaptation. Table 4 and Appendix C.1 present different round-specific configurations whose alignment is unverified here; we do not merge them into one quantitative trajectory.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: LoCoMo; LongMemEval; MemoryAgentBench; PersonaMind. Initial hierarchical memory architecture g0 with executable layer methods.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Evolution rewrites construction, indexing, retrieval and routing programs within the supplied hierarchy. Its initial architecture already supports threshold-based adaptive reading; the evolved artifact changes those methods rather than introducing adaptive depth from scratch.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Initial hierarchy design is not itself discovered. The study separately analyzes question-level and record-disjoint splits, acceptance gates and cross-benchmark transfer; no universal optimal depth follows.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: OfficeQA. OpenClaw with initial skills, AGENTS.md, SOUL.md and tools.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Figure 3(a) expands an existing financial-metrics skill: fix the statistic and operands before computing, distinguish changes in shares from growth rates, specify the denominator, convert log returns when the requested quantity requires it, and check constants and revised values against the corpus. These are reusable instructions, not enforced executable checks. The old skill already requests corpus-grounded currency conversion; that inherited instruction is not a new discovery. Selected skills are subsequently tested in other execution frameworks.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Appendix A, Figure 3(a) supplies the inspected before/after artifact; the individual rules are not separately ablated. Framework transfer reuses learned skills rather than adding independent discoveries, and the illustration alone does not establish each line's presence in the best final checkpoint.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: MuSiQue and HotpotQA within a textual task stream. A frozen model with editable task interface, memory, capabilities and routing.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Sequential harness updates are tested on current tasks and historical anchors; the study contrasts strict retention with permissive adaptation.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Separate adaptation, validation and test examples support a continual-evolution experiment, but no final QA-specific executable diff is exposed in this record.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: TaskCraft; GAIA; WebWalkerQA; xBench-DeepSearch. AgentKB or a simple few-shot experience memory.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Search changes memory encoding, retrieval and management programs. From a lightweight AgentKB-style seed without its offline knowledge base, Cerebra adds reusable tool and knowledge distillation and working-memory maintenance; other reported branches include Riva and Lightweight.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: WebWalkerQA and xBench use architectures evolved on TaskCraft. Their evaluations are frozen transfer evidence, not independent in-benchmark evolution runs.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: GAIA. HarnessX task configuration with prompts, processors, slots and tool resources.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: The GAIA evolution analysis reports shipped prompt, processor, configuration and tool edits, addressing blocked sources alongside reasoning and parsing failures.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Lever-level statistics do not identify one universally retained retrieval tool. The same task pool is evaluated during search; this supports benchmark adaptation rather than a sealed generalization test.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: GAIA. A neutral observation–action prompt, default runner settings and no custom processors.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Trajectory analysis proposes prompt fragments, knowledge, processors and settings; replay removes inert or invalid processors before the composer assembles candidates.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: GAIA is evaluated transductively. Appendix C.4 documents answer-copy exposure despite blocking known mirrors, including a returned processor's guidance about dataset mirrors. The score does not establish clean unseen-question generalization.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: SearchQA. OpenClaw with an unoptimized skill and tool configuration.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Failed executions and validated answer-assisted reference trajectories drive persistent skill-directory and harness updates. The resulting SearchQA skills are frozen for cross-framework evaluation.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The SearchQA scores and transfer establish task-level evolution evidence, but the OfficeQA or enterprise SQL example must not be relabeled as a SearchQA-specific final edit.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: WebArena websites and held-out web tasks. A web agent using low-level browser actions.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Practice discovers and refines executable Playwright APIs. In the published delete_merged_branches case, a global textbox selector matches both GitLab search and the confirmation field, causing a strict-mode error. The repaired API scopes the textbox and confirmation button to the deletion dialog; the agent patches its persistent knowledge base.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: Functions persist beyond their discovery tasks. This is component-level skill improvement, not self-rewriting of the outer optimizer; dynamic-site skills can fail when realistic test inputs are unavailable.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: WebArena-Infinity. Solver without an evolved skill library.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Online reflection is compiled into reusable general and task-type skills. Published web cases include disabling an existing auto label, preserving corporate email domains, and archiving qualifying read-important emails.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The main sequential protocol learns between batches. Frozen transfer is evaluated separately; the web examples are advisory procedures, not verified new browser APIs.

sections.label: Setting and seed
sections.text: WebShop. A neutral turn-protocol prompt and action–observation chat loop, with no initial processors or benchmark-specific prompt content.

sections.label: Reported evolution
sections.text: Repeated failure analysis is converted into reusable prompt, knowledge, processor and configuration components, with candidate selection under the WebShop task evaluator.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The study reports an inductive WebShop configuration, but the concrete login processor described for AppWorld is not a WebShop discovery. A complete selected WebShop diff is not established here.

sections.label: Evidence and limits
